notes: \cpara{Introduces the commenter Kurige again, with a first quotation.}

\cpara{The sentence matches Kurige's comment on ``No, Really, I've Deceived Myself.'' The comment's next paragraph says what ``double-think'' meant there: holding both that God instilled a sense of right and wrong and that morality evolved, and ``These two beliefs are not contradictory, but the complexity lies in reconciling the two.'' Orwell's doublethink is ``the power of holding two contradictory beliefs in one's mind simultaneously.'' Kurige called the view ``Orwellian'' but used the word more loosely, for two accounts that need reconciling.}
\cpara{The reply asks how one can believe what one knows is double-think. It reads the word in Orwell's sense (see the previous note).}
\cpara{From Kurige's reply to ``Moore's Paradox.'' The wording matches.}

\cpara{Kurige's second sentence says the decision does not make God exist. That is true of every belief, accurate ones included. On the author's own account of evidence in ``What Is Evidence?'', a belief is correlated with reality by being caused by it, not by causing it. So the sentence does not say the belief is uncorrelated. The post's reading rests on ``chose,'' and the same comment compares the belief to a scientist's belief in the Higgs boson: ``The scientist has evidence that such a particle exists.''}

\cpara{Asks why knowing that a map has no reason to match the territory does not end belief in it. ``What Is Evidence?'' (2007) had said that if you feel this ``on a gut level,'' you will ``automatically stop believing.''}
\cpara{The answer, from the comments: apparently not.}
\cpara{First explanation, hedged (``may be''): the account given in ``Moore's Paradox.''}

\cpara{Second explanation, hedged (``may just be''), offered ``contrary to the indignation I initially wanted to put forward'': it may be ``quite easy'' not to go from what an accurate map would say to believing it.}

\cpara{The quoted sentence is from ``Doublethink'' (2007). The author now says the sentence was partly an attempt at a self-fulfilling prophecy. ``Doublethink'' offered it as fact, and ``Belief in Self-Deception,'' four days before this post, repeated it (``you can't just choose to believe the sky is green'').}

\cpara{The advice, hedged (``may be wise''): repeat to yourself that you cannot double-think. It amounts to adopting a belief for its effects, close to what ``Doublethink'' argued against when it rejected the idea that you ``can decide which cognitive biases should govern you.'' What differs is that this belief is meant to make itself true once held.}
\cpara{The claimed effect is stated without a hedge (``you will indeed be less likely to fool yourself successfully''), and no evidence is given for it.}
\cpara{Restates the effect and lists the failures it guards against: real belief, Moore's paradox, belief in belief, belief in self-deception.}
\cpara{The first of three clauses, each a thing to keep telling yourself: deep down you will know.}
\cpara{The second: you would see your own false map as false.}
\cpara{The third: reflective consistency would end the belief.}
\cpara{The conclusion of the clauses, hedged (``may''): you will fail to deceive yourself.}
\cpara{Restates the advice as a command. The next line drops the hedge: ``and it will be!''}
\cpara{Ends by asking whether this is positive or negative thinking, and calls it, with ``seems,'' a wise precaution.}
